overview: Liberia declared independence in 1847, before this map record begins. Its history joins indigenous African communities with settlers from the United States and their descendants. Republican promises coexisted with unequal access to power; later coups and civil wars were followed by peacebuilding in which women’s organizations played an important role.

periods.title: An independent republic with unequal power
periods.summary: The republic’s institutions developed alongside contested relations between settler-descended elites and indigenous communities.

periods.title: Coup, upheaval and civil wars
periods.summary: The 1980 coup ended the first republic; war and peace negotiations later transformed national life.

periods.title: Peacebuilding and continuing society
periods.summary: The 2003 agreement, women’s organizing and reconstruction opened a new chapter, with UNMIL’s mandate ending in 2018.

sections.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample

items.text: The American Colonization Society helped establish settlements for free and formerly enslaved Black Americans on the West African coast. It was a private organization. The independent republic proclaimed in 1847 developed special U.S. connections, but was not simply a U.S. state overseas.

“a Free, Sovereign and Independent State” appears in the 1847 constitution’s preamble. This original English sample states the founders’ claim to govern their own republic. In plain language, they were declaring that another country should not rule them.

The constitution divided government into legislative, executive and judicial branches and protected publication and political discussion. Its written promises provide a way to ask how later governments treated rights in practice.

David McClellan’s 1850 map includes water-depth soundings near the coast and sketches of mountains. It also marks indigenous communities and new settlements. A map could help a ship approach land while recording the ambitions and interests of its makers.

Customs duties on traded goods supplied much of the early government’s revenue. Indigenous traders and British merchants disputed the colonization society’s authority to collect them. Arguments over ordinary cargo and taxes helped push the settlers towards independence.

A Dan feasting spoon at the Metropolitan Museum has a handle carved as human legs and feet. Dated broadly from the nineteenth to mid-twentieth century, it belongs to an artistic tradition associated with Dan communities in Liberia and neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire.

Such ceremonial ladles honoured women known for generous hospitality. A titleholder organized important meals and fed travellers; successful farming helped make that generosity possible. This was a spoon with social responsibilities far beyond stirring one person’s lunch.

sections.title: Political voice, peace and school life

items.text: Indigenous people were brought into an indirect relationship with central government through local officials in 1904, and voting rights expanded in 1946. These changes show why independence in 1847 did not immediately give everyone an equal political voice.

Leymah Gbowee helped bring Christian and Muslim women together in a nonviolent peace movement. Women demonstrated publicly and travelled to the 2003 talks in Accra to press negotiators towards agreement. Organizing across religious lines became a practical political achievement.

Gbowee and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize with Yemen’s Tawakkul Karman. The award recognized efforts for women’s safety and participation in peacebuilding. Women were shaping decisions about the country’s future, alongside caring for families affected by war.

At D. Tweh Memorial School in New Kru Town, pupils joined handwashing activities in October 2025. One student described reminding people to wash after using the toilet. The everyday work of protecting classmates included speaking up as well as turning on a tap.

In Zwedru, students marked the same handwashing day with drama, music and football. A lesson about soap could arrive through a performance or a game. UNICEF’s account records these specific activities as part of a wider effort to improve hygiene.

ending.text: Liberia’s first republic ended in the 1980 coup, but Liberia itself continued. The 2003 peace agreement and later reconstruction brought further change; the UN peacekeeping mandate ended in March 2018. Its communities continue building institutions and everyday lives after the wars.
